part_b_mcq: Which feature distinguishes a productive elongation complex from a promoter-bound closed complex?
A growing RNA paired to template DNA
An intact DNA duplex throughout the active center
An obligatory free RNA primer
A translating ribosome as a catalytic subunit
An elongation complex contains the nascent RNA–DNA hybrid. A closed promoter complex has not opened the DNA; neither a free primer nor a ribosome is a required RNAP subunit.
Which RNA end receives each new nucleotide?
5′ end
3′ end
Both ends alternately
Either end depending on sigma
The terminal 3′ hydroxyl attacks the incoming NTP alpha phosphate; the 5′ end is not extended.
What becomes of the beta and gamma phosphates during normal incorporation?
Both remain in the RNA backbone
They are released as pyrophosphate
They become an amino acid
They are hydrolyzed by Rho before incorporation
The alpha phosphate becomes part of the new phosphodiester bond; beta and gamma leave as PPi. Rho is not needed.
A DNA coding strand reads 5′-ACGTTG-3′. What RNA sequence is produced across it?
5′-UGCAAC-3′
5′-ACGUUG-3′
5′-CAACGU-3′
5′-ACGTTG-3′
The coding strand and RNA have the same sequence in the same orientation except T becomes U. The other choices confuse complement, orientation or RNA bases.
Which statement about the transcription bubble is most accurate?
It grows to the length of the whole transcript
It is identical to the entire RNA product
It is a local region of strand separation that moves with RNAP
It remains at the promoter
The bubble is renewed as downstream DNA opens and upstream DNA reanneals; only a short hybrid remains inside.
What is the primary role of the RNA–DNA hybrid during elongation?
It permanently attaches RNA to the chromosome
It supplies covalent links between DNA and RNA
It contributes to correct alignment and complex stability
It replaces the DNA template
Complementary noncovalent pairing positions RNA and helps stabilize the complex; RNA must eventually be released.
Which energy source is directly used for formation of a new RNA phosphodiester bond?
The triphosphate of the incoming NTP
A separate ATP hydrolyzed by sigma
GTP hydrolysis by a ribosome
ATP hydrolysis by Rho at every position
The incoming NTP supplies the reactive phosphate group and releases PPi; other motors use energy independently.
What is the best meaning of RNAP processivity?
Number of promoters in the genome
Rate of ATP synthesis
Ability to continue repeated incorporation without dissociation
Ability of a ribosome to select a codon
Processivity concerns persistence on the substrate; speed and promoter selection are distinct.
Which observation most directly supports a reversible pause rather than termination?
RNA is short at one early time point
The short associated RNA later extends in a chase
Total protein decreases
The DNA contains adenine
Extension of the same associated intermediate shows that the elongation complex remained productive or recovered.
During backtracking, what can prevent further addition?
The RNA 3′ end leaves productive alignment
DNA becomes permanently covalently linked to RNA
Sigma cleaves the chromosome
The ribosome removes all NTPs
Displacement of the 3′ end prevents normal catalysis. Recovery can involve forward movement or RNA cleavage.
What is a principal function of bacterial Gre factors?
Synthesis of ATP
Stimulating RNA cleavage in backtracked RNAP
Recognizing all promoters
Hydrolyzing a terminator DNA strand
Gre factors stimulate transcript cleavage, restoring a usable 3′ end; they are not promoter recognition factors or DNA nucleases.
Which pattern is most characteristic of an intrinsic terminator RNA?
Poly(A) followed by a random stem
A stem-loop followed by a U-rich segment
A start codon followed by a stop codon
An obligatory C-rich rut site alone
The stem-loop and downstream U-rich region form the classical combination. Rut relates to Rho recognition.
Which DNA template segment produces a U-rich RNA tract?
T-rich DNA
A-rich DNA
G-rich DNA
C-rich DNA
Template adenines pair with incoming UTP. Coding-strand thymidines represent the same signal on the opposite strand.
What is the usual outcome of a disruptive mutation in an essential intrinsic terminator stem?
Increased readthrough, other conditions equal
Obligatory new initiation
RNA converted to DNA
Immediate RNA cleavage at every U
Weakening the stem can decrease termination. It does not directly create a promoter or change polymerization into DNA synthesis.
Why can NusA enhance some intrinsic terminators without contradicting their classification?
NusA is the same protein as Rho
Intrinsic means no RNA is involved
Accessory factors can help a sequence-driven mechanism
NusA is always an obligatory ATP motor
Intrinsic signals can function without obligatory Rho; cellular factors may increase efficiency.
Which statement correctly describes Rho?
A six-subunit RNA-directed ATP-dependent motor
A bacterial DNA polymerase
A stop codon
A constitutive catalytic RNAP subunit
Rho is a separate protein factor with RNA-binding and ATP-dependent motor activity.
What properties often favor rut recognition?
A fully base-paired G-rich RNA region
Accessible C-rich, G-poor RNA
A required DNA TATA box
An exposed DNA replication origin
Accessibility and composition of nascent RNA matter; rut is not a universal fixed DNA promoter motif.
In the classical model Rho travels in which direction on RNA?
From the DNA template 5′ end to its 3′ end independently of RNA
No preferred direction
Rho approaches the growing 3′ region by moving from an upstream RNA site toward the 3′ end.
Which observation supports Rho-dependent termination most directly?
The sequence has any hairpin
Adding active Rho selectively increases released short RNA
A stop codon is present
The RNA is translated
A factor-addition effect with release controls supports a causal role for Rho; sequence alone does not establish it.
A premature translation stop can increase downstream Rho action primarily because:
The ribosome becomes RNA polymerase
More RNA can become accessible to Rho
The stop codon always destroys DNA
Rho recognizes stop codons as DNA cleavage signals
Loss of translating ribosome occupancy can expose RNA. Effects vary with the transcript and available termination signals.
Rifampicin primarily binds which target?
Bacterial RNAP beta subunit
Bacterial 30S ribosomal decoding site
DNA minor groove exclusively
Rho ATPase as its canonical target
The drug binds RpoB near the path of the initially growing RNA; it is not primarily a translation or Rho inhibitor.
Why is rifampicin often described as a transcription initiation inhibitor?
It prevents every initial DNA contact
It blocks productive early RNA extension
It removes the 5′ cap from bacterial RNA
It always releases mature elongation complexes
Initial short RNA may still form, but extension beyond a few nucleotides is obstructed. Mature elongation complexes are generally much less affected.
Actinomycin D differs from rifampicin in that its characteristic direct target is:
DNA
The bacterial ribosomal A site
Rho exclusively
The sigma factor promoter-binding domain
DNA binding/intercalation can impede transcription across bacterial and eukaryotic systems; this is not the RpoB pocket mechanism.
What is an appropriate inference if a transcription inhibitor causes a delayed fall in protein synthesis?
Its direct target must be a ribosome
Existing RNA can continue to support translation temporarily
All existing RNA disappears at drug addition
The inhibitor necessarily cleaves DNA
Reduced new RNA production eventually limits templates for translation; the time delay does not identify a ribosomal target.
Which statement about termination and RNA processing is correct?
Every mature RNA 3′ end is the initial RNAP release site
RNA processing and termination can produce coincident ends
Processing always requires Rho
Termination is synonymous with phosphodiester cleavage
A mapped 3′ end can reflect release or subsequent processing. Additional observations are needed.
Which property is not universally shared by all prokaryotes?
Use of nucleic acids
Template-directed transcription
Bacterial Rho-dependent termination
Phosphodiester-linked RNA
Archaea have distinct transcription machinery; even bacteria vary in their use of Rho.
assertion_reason: Assertion: A 1,000-nt transcript does not require a 1,000-bp transcription bubble. Reason: DNA reanneals behind the moving transcription complex.
The bubble is maintained locally and moves along the DNA rather than growing with the RNA.
Assertion: A hairpin can pause RNAP without necessarily terminating transcription. Reason: Pausing and irreversible RNA release are different molecular outcomes.
A paused complex can recover; release needs further destabilization.
Assertion: Removing ATP from a transcription reaction specifically tests Rho activity. Reason: ATP is also an RNA polymerase substrate.
ATP withdrawal can alter polymerization itself, confounding interpretation.
Assertion: Rifampicin immediately eliminates all RNA in a bacterial cell. Reason: Pre-existing RNA can persist and established complexes may finish transcription.
Blocking new initiation is not instantaneous RNA degradation.
Assertion: Intrinsic termination cannot be modulated by proteins. Reason: NusA can assist the function of some intrinsic terminators.
Factor-independent capability does not imply immunity to regulation.
Assertion: A high RNAP occupancy peak proves increased transcription initiation. Reason: Slow passage can raise local occupancy.
A residence-time effect may create the peak without increased incoming flux.
multiple_matching: Select all correct statements: (i) Rho binds RNA; (ii) Rho is a ribosome; (iii) Rho uses ATP; (iv) rut need not coincide with the release site.
Rho is a distinct ATP-dependent factor that can engage upstream RNA.

Match each term: A. Rifampicin; B. Actinomycin D; C. Gre factor; D. NusA. Targets/functions: 1. DNA binding; 2. early RNAP extension inhibition; 3. RNA cleavage stimulation; 4. facilitation of selected intrinsic terminators.
The first two are inhibitors with distinct direct targets; the latter two modulate elongation or termination.
Select all true: (i) template A specifies RNA U; (ii) template T specifies RNA A; (iii) RNA grows at its 5′ end; (iv) RNAP reads template 3′→5′.
Complementary decoding and antiparallel orientation are compatible with 3′-end addition.

Match event A. Pause; B. Release; C. Initiation block; D. RNA degradation to observation 1. Existing RNA shortened after synthesis; 2. Associated intermediate can extend; 3. New productive starts fail; 4. Free nonextendable product.
The categories describe different physical outcomes and can be distinguished experimentally.

Select all valid controls for a proposed Rho-dependent termination assay: (i) no Rho; (ii) active Rho add-back; (iii) test for RNA degradation; (iv) omit all template and interpret the missing band as proof of Rho dependence.
No-template may be a general background control, but loss of signal there cannot prove Rho dependence.
part_c: A 2,100-nt region is copied at 70 nt/s, excluding three pauses of 3, 5 and 7 s. Calculate total time and average velocity.
The productive rate excludes pause time; dividing length by elapsed time includes it.
At a pause, 25% remain after 10 s, with single first-order escape and no new entry. Find half-time and escape rate.
Two half-lives reduce the population to one-quarter. If release also occurs, the fitted rate is total exit.
A Rho motor is 90 nt behind RNAP. Motor speed 60 nt/s, RNAP speed 30 nt/s. Under constant-speed catch-up assumptions, when do they meet?
Relative speed is 30 nt/s, so 90/30 = 3. Meeting is not guaranteed termination.
Rho is 48 nt away at the start of a pause and moves at 24 nt/s. Does a 1.5-s pause permit catch-up? What about 3 s?
No for 1.5 s; yes for 3 s in the model.
The distance requires 48/24 = 2 s. Loading delays and conformational states are ignored.
Termination and readthrough molecule counts are 135 and 45. Calculate both fractions.
TE = 75%; readthrough = 25%.
Divide each count by 180; their sum is 100% only if all relevant products are counted.
Terminated 150-nt RNA has signal 900; readthrough 450-nt RNA has signal 900. Uniform signal per residue. Calculate corrected termination efficiency.
Molecule equivalents are 900/150 = 6 and 900/450 = 2; 6/(6+2) = 0.75, not 50%.
A single decision state has kt = 2 s⁻¹ and ke = 6 s⁻¹. What are termination probability and mean residence time?
Competing rates give kt/(kt+ke); mean dwell time is 1/(kt+ke).
Two sequential terminators stop 60% and 75% of arrivals. With no new initiation or other loss, what percentage reads through both?
Readthrough = (1−0.60)(1−0.75) = 0.40×0.25 = 0.10; total termination is 90%.
Under an ideal instantaneous block, RNA drops from 960 to 120 molecules in 9 min. Find apparent half-life.
3 min.
960/120 = 8 = 2³, so three half-lives occupy nine minutes. Run-off could bias real measurements.
A polymerase has 1,500 nt remaining when rifampicin is added. At 50 nt/s and assuming no effect on established elongation, when can it finish?
The block prevents new productive starts, not necessarily ongoing extension; 1,500/50 = 30.
A mutant stem arm gives termination 12% versus WT 80%; double compensatory mutant gives 73%. What is the strongest inference?
Stem complementarity is important; the rescue supports RNA structure rather than a uniquely required original base sequence.
The rescue does not prove all sequence-specific effects are absent, and 73% is not identical to WT.
A candidate site gives 8% short RNA without Rho, 70% with WT Rho, and 9% with an RNA-binding but ATPase-impaired Rho. Explain.
A large Rho-dependent component requires functional ATPase activity, assuming variants are stable and active amounts comparable.
RNA binding alone is insufficient; short product release and degradation controls are still necessary.
A 100-nt RNA accumulates at 5 s, then most becomes 300-nt RNA in a single-round chase. What is the interpretation?
A reversible pause is supported.
Conversion of the labeled associated product into longer RNA distinguishes pausing from irreversible release.
A mutation reduces downstream RNA but leaves upstream RNA unchanged. Rho impairment rescues the downstream signal. What mechanism is supported?
Premature Rho-dependent termination, possibly due to exposed RNA.
Alternative effects on stability or internal promoter activity require controls; the rescue strengthens the termination hypothesis.
Drug X inhibits only new productive starts in a defined assay. Drug Y binds duplex DNA and reduces passage of established complexes. Identify likely examples.
X: rifampicin; Y: actinomycin D.
The timing and binding evidence distinguish the direct targets. A growth effect alone would not identify the drugs.
A polymerase mutant doubles occupancy at a locus but halves downstream transcript output. What competing interpretations should be considered?
Increased dwell time, stalling or termination may reduce productive flux.
Occupancy depends on arrival and residence; it does not establish increased initiation.
Two RNA ends are identical in sequence; one is produced in vitro by RNAP release, the other by cleavage of a longer RNA. Can 3′-end mapping alone distinguish them?
No.
Both have the same mapped end. Nascent transcription and release/cleavage evidence are needed.
An RNA production rate is 100 molecules/min and readthrough is 0.2. A mutant changes readthrough to 0.5, leaving decay constant and initiation unchanged. Predict relative downstream steady-state RNA.
2.5-fold increase.
Flux rises from 20 to 50 molecules/min; at identical first-order loss the steady-state ratio is 50/20.
A mutation slows RNAP but leaves Rho motion unchanged; under catch-up assumptions, what is the predicted effect on Rho-dependent termination?
More opportunity for Rho encounter and potentially increased termination.
The change is conditional on accessible RNA and susceptible RNAP, and does not guarantee release.
A drug inhibits RNA production in intact cells, but purified RNAP from treated cells functions normally without drug. Is the direct target established?
No.
Removing drug or cellular context may restore activity; compare direct target binding and defined functional reactions with drug present.
